name: PT Sumber Energi Andalan Tbk

frontmatter.title: Sumber Energi Andalan: a coal-port stake at the market's own discount
frontmatter.summary: ITMA owns a 30.0% stake in PT Mitratama Perkasa, the unlisted coal-port landlord of South Kalimantan, carried at US$201.0m of US$215.6m parent equity. The market already applies a 74.1% discount to that book and we find no dated catalyst to narrow it: after the 20% liquidity haircut the twelve-month value is Rp905 against Rp1,010, a -10.4% return.
thesis: The value is one unlisted asset: ITMA's 30.0% stake in PT Mitratama Perkasa, whose coal handling and port assets in South Kalimantan are carried at US$201.0m of the US$215.6m parent equity [S2].
The base case holds the discount the market already applies, 74.1%. The house default is that holding-company discounts persist, and this company offers no dated catalyst to narrow one [S2][S0].
The marks are audited carrying values, so the parts sum to parent equity by construction: this is a price-to-book target with a governance discount, not an independent appraisal of the port [S2].
The 20% haircut is a single, separate charge. The stock turns over IDR102.0m a day, far below the fund's floor, so the name is watch-only whatever the target says [S0].

What would change the view is cash actually upstreamed: a first dividend from Mitratama Perkasa, or a sale of the stake near carrying value, with the FY2026 audited accounts as the first dated test [S2].

catalysts.event: Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia begins acting as the single intermediary for coal exports, with price negotiation left to the miners and the ports
FY2026 audited results: the first dated point at which a Mitratama Perkasa dividend or an asset sale would become visible, the only events that would justify a narrower discount

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Sumber Energi Andalan with a REDUCE rating and a twelve-month value of Rp905 a share, -10.4% against the Rp1,010 close on 6 November 2026 [S0]. ITMA is not an operating company in any useful sense: it is a listed wrapper around a 30.0% stake in PT Mitratama Perkasa, the unlisted company that owns and leases the coal handling ports, coal processing plants and barge unloaders at Asam-Asam and West Mulia in South Kalimantan, plus a small power-plant rental fleet and a loss-making oxygen joint venture [S2][F6][F7][F8]. Those three marks, less the obligations left in the balance sheet, account for the whole of the parent's US$215.6m of equity [S2].

The method is simpler than a sum of the parts sounds, and we label it honestly. We mark Mitratama Perkasa at the audited equity-method carrying value of US$201.0m, the oxygen joint venture at US$26.3m and the rental and LNG subsidiaries at their net fixed assets of US$25.5m, deduct the holding-company obligations that remain in the consolidated balance sheet, and arrive back at audited parent equity by construction [S2]. Because the deduction is the residual of the same balance sheet, the tie-out is an identity, not a corroboration: the target is a price-to-book mark, with a governance discount for the structure and a separate liquidity haircut [S2]. On that book we apply a 74.1% discount and the 20% liquidity charge, and the result is Rp905.

The variant view is not that the parts are worth more than book. It is that the market's 74.1% discount is the right starting point: the governance record and the absence of any cash-upstream channel justify a discount of that order, and there is no dated event in our sources that would narrow it in the base case [S2][S0]. The house card treats a persistent discount as the base rate, so we do not underwrite a re-rating: the base holds the market's 74.1%, the bull is the only path that narrows, and it is conditional on a cash event at the FY2026 accounts [S2].

What moves the value is narrow and identifiable. First, whether Mitratama Perkasa ever pays a dividend up to ITMA: the carrying value moves only with share of profit and other comprehensive income, and the note shows no distribution in either year [S2]. Second, the associate's own balance sheet, which carries US$243.2m of liabilities against ITMA's US$16.9m of debt — a refinancing there, or a covenant test, can impair the mark [S2]. Third, the LNG plant still in construction and the Sangatta joint venture, both carried at cost [S2][F7][F33]. Fourth, the discount itself, a governance judgement rather than an earnings one [S2].

The strongest case against us is that we are valuing a claim on cash we cannot see. Operating cash flow was negative in FY2025, free cash flow was US$-5.4m, the parent has paid no dividend from the shares Astrindo holds, and the only cash that could reach shareholders would have to be upstreamed through a controller with capital needs of its own [S2]. That is why the bear case carries a quarter of the probability and a value of Rp694, and why the stock is watch-only on the fund's liquidity floor rather than a position we could size [S2][S0].

PT Sumber Energi Andalan listed in 1990 and spent two decades as a small trading, consulting and contracting vehicle for the mining and energy sectors before it became an energy holding [S2]. Its present shape was set in 2012, when it bought 30.0% of PT Mitratama Perkasa for US$1.0, and in 2018, when PT Astrindo Nusantara Infrastruktur Tbk acquired a controlling block and displaced Trust Energy Resources as the controlling shareholder [S2][F31][F22]. Astrindo holds 41.9% of the shares at the end of 2025; the blocking register shows three further non-controlling blocks above five per cent — Fersindo Nusa Jaya, Trukindo Persada Sejahtera and Majukarya Mandiri Indonesia — and the balance, 32.3%, is held by the public in blocks below five per cent [S2][F34][F35]. The company reports in US dollars, which is unusual on IDX and follows from the fact that its contracts and its associate are dollar-denominated [S2].

The first and dominant block is the Mitratama Perkasa stake. Mitratama Perkasa is a coal-infrastructure company in South Kalimantan with five fully operational assets: the Asam-Asam coal processing plant and overland conveyor, the Asam-Asam coal handling port, the West Mulia processing plant and conveyor, the West Mulia coal port, and a continuous barge unloader [S2]. It does not mine coal. It leases the ports and the crusher facilities to coal companies and charges for coal processing, handling, barging, storage and loading [S2]. The Asam-Asam port has coal handling capacity of 12.0 Mt/yr a year, with a jetty, berthing and mooring dolphins, conveyor belts, dust suppression and a reclaim feeder — long-lived, location-bound infrastructure that sits between the mines of Tanah Laut and the barges that feed the export trade [S2][F20]. Mitratama Perkasa reported total assets of US$977.2m and liabilities of US$243.2m at the end of 2025 and earned US$11.9m, which is a thin return on its own equity base [S2]. Nusantara Pratama Indah holds the balance of Mitratama Perkasa's shares [S2].

The second block is a power-plant rental business. Through PT Indopower Energi Abadi, ITMA manages power plants exceeding a total capacity of 60.0 MW across Indonesia, with PT PLN (Persero) and PT Pertamina (Persero) as its principal clients [S2][F19]. The fleet is spread across Sembakung in North Kalimantan, Jeranjang in Lombok and Batam in the Riau Islands [S2]. The assets that drove the FY2025 revenue step-up were a diesel plant at Jeranjang and a gas engine plant at Batam, both of which moved from construction into service during the year [S2]. Rental services produced 77.3% of FY2025 revenue, US$1.6m, from almost nothing in the prior year, alongside mobilisation revenue and a related-party consulting line [S2][F15][F30].

The third block is a joint venture. PT Oksigen Natural Esa is carried at US$26.3m for a stake in a prefabrication construction plant at Sangatta in East Kalimantan [S2][F7]. It is not yet operating: the joint venture result was US$-1.8m in FY2025 after a small profit in the prior year, and its most recent disclosed revenue was negligible against its asset base [S2]. Alongside these, PT Para Amartha LNG is building a liquefaction and storage facility at Wunut in East Java to serve industrial gas customers in Java; it is a development project, not a revenue line [S2]. The fixed-asset note puts US$20.1m of the group's US$25.5m of net fixed assets in construction in progress, including an LNG processing plant carried at US$20.0m and ninety per cent complete, with a target date that has already slipped from February 2025 to October 2026 [S2][F8][F32][F33].

The strategy the board describes is asset utilisation rather than expansion: running the rental fleet at high utilisation, holding the existing power-supply contracts, and letting the port assets earn on throughput [S2]. The company is a challenger in coal logistics, not a leader — Mitratama Perkasa competes with the integrated port and barging arms of the coal groups and with independent terminal operators, and its Asam-Asam capacity is a rounding error against Indonesia's national output [S2][S7]. Its advantage is location and installed infrastructure, not scale [S2].

ITMA's economics are tied to Indonesian coal volumes rather than to the coal price. Mitratama Perkasa is paid for handling tonnes, so what matters is how much coal moves through South Kalimantan, not what the coal is worth at the mine gate [S2]. That distinction matters in a year when the price has moved sharply and the volume has not.

Indonesia produced 817 Mt of coal in 2025 and supplied 540 Mt of the world seaborne coal trade [S7][F23][F26]. The government's own framing is that the country's volume pushed prices to their lowest levels of the year, and that the policy response was to raise the reference coal price and cut production to rebalance the market; the energy minister now cites high-calorie coal at US$154/t, with state non-tax revenue from coal rising even as output fell [S7][F25]. That is the deck the port assets sit on: a supply-disciplined coal market with a firmer price and a smaller volume [S7].

The volume path is the live question, and the figures need care. Production through July was 424 Mt, an average below the prior year's monthly pace, which is consistent with a quota-constrained year rather than a demand collapse [S6][S7][F38]. The ministry's latest count is 567 Mt, which its report describes as 77.0% of the target; that completion rate implies a plan well above the 600 Mt figure the annual report cited as the government's "more controlled" planning number, so the annual-report figure is stale and we do not build a headwind argument on it [S7][F24][F27][F37]. On either reading, 2026 output is tracking below the 2025 total of 817 Mt; for a port landlord that is a modest throughput headwind, not a tailwind, and the minister's statement that quotas and work plans will be adjusted upward as prices improve is the swing factor the other way [S7][F23]. We treat the ministry's current plan as the base and the quota debate as the swing.

Regulation is the second driver and it touches the export chain directly. From 1 January 2027, PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia is to act as the single intermediary in the export of strategic resources including coal, sitting between seller and buyer to check transaction documents for under-invoicing, while the government states that price negotiation and the commercial relationship remain with the companies [S5]. For a coal-port landlord this is a documentation and compliance layer rather than a price mechanism, but it adds a state counterparty to the export chain and it is the largest change to that channel in the period our sources cover [S5].

The competitive structure of coal logistics is moderately attractive but not a moat. Coal has to be crushed, conveyed, stockpiled and loaded, and the assets that do it are capital-intensive, permitted and hard to relocate, which gives an incumbent terminal pricing power within its catchment [S2]. Against that, the customer base is a handful of coal companies and traders with real bargaining power over throughput fees, new capacity can be built when volumes justify it, and the whole chain depends on a single commodity whose volumes the state now manages [S7][S5]. Five forces, briefly: buyer power high because customers are concentrated and mobile between terminals; supplier power low because the inputs are labour and spare parts; threat of new entry moderate because permits and capital are barriers but the assets are replicable; threat of substitutes low because Kalimantan coal still moves by barge; rivalry moderate because terminals compete on location and tariff [S2].

The power-rental business has a different structure: it is a leasing business to two state-owned offtakers, PLN and Pertamina, where the moat is the installed fleet and the contract, and the risk is renewal and re-pricing [S2]. Its returns depend on utilisation and on the fuel cost the contracts pass through, which is why the segment's margin moved so much in FY2025 as the engines came into service [S2][F15].

Indonesian coal logistics has historically been a landlord business: the mines carry the price risk and the terminals earn a handling fee per tonne, usually with a take-or-pay or minimum-throughput element. That structure means terminal earnings are more stable than miner earnings but also capped, and the equity market has generally valued terminals on throughput and contract duration rather than on the coal price. This is background on how the segment usually works, not a statement about Mitratama Perkasa's specific contracts, which are not disclosed in the annual report.

ITMA's reported revenue is small and its reported profit is not operating profit. Revenue was US$2.1m in FY2025, up 113.9% from US$1.0m, as the rental fleet moved from construction into service and the revenue mix rotated from maintenance work to equipment rental [S2][S0]. Rental services alone contributed US$1.6m, or 77.3% of revenue, with mobilisation and consulting making up the rest [S2][F15][F30]. The prior year was a maintenance-contract year, which is why the comparison is so violent and why the FY2024 gross margin is not a guide to anything [S2].

Margins fell as the mix changed. Gross margin was 40.7% in FY2025 against a consulting-heavy base in FY2024, because hired contractor cost and equipment depreciation entered cost of revenue with the rental contracts [S2]. Depreciation is the line the data pack gets wrong: the pack carries a negligible charge, while the fixed-asset note shows US$0.2m of depreciation charged in FY2025, of which US$0.2m sits in cost of revenue [S2][F3][F16]. We restate history from the note, which lowers EBITDA optics but is the honest charge on US$25.5m of rental engines and LNG plant [S2]. On the restated base, EBITDA was US$0.8m and EBIT US$0.5m [S2].

The profit line is almost entirely equity-accounted. The share of Mitratama Perkasa's profit was US$3.6m in FY2025, against a US$-1.8m share of the oxygen joint venture's result, so the below-EBIT block contributed roughly the whole of pre-tax profit [S2][F13][F14]. Net profit attributable to shareholders was US$1.8m, a return on US$215.6m of equity of 0.8% [S2]. That is the central analytical fact about this company: the parent earns a thin return on a large book because the book is a port stake earning a low return on its own assets, and the parent's own operating business does not cover its cost of capital [S2].

Cash is the weak point. Operating cash flow was negative in FY2025, free cash flow was US$-5.4m after US$6.0m of equipment purchases, and gross debt rose to US$16.9m — term loans from Bank Mandiri and Bank JTrust — against US$0.5m of cash [S2][S0]. Net debt was US$16.3m, but that understates the claims: the balance sheet also carries US$23.9m of long-term non-trade payables to third parties, which is why the holding-company deduction in our sum of the parts is larger than the debt line [S2][F28]. The company funds its capex with term debt and with customer advances; operating working capital is negative because the rental business runs on prepayments [S2].

Our forecast reproduces FY2025's economics rather than extrapolating the equipment-purchase years. Revenue is set at US$3.0m for FY2026E, essentially the twelve months to September 2026 already reported in the data pack, after which growth fades as the fleet reaches contracted capacity [S0]. We hold the FY2025 gross margin and the FY2025 SG&A ratio rather than assume operating leverage; capex falls from a completion tail to maintenance levels because the engines are already bought [S2]. The result is EBITDA of US$1.0m and net profit of US$1.9m. The dividend record needs one correction: the policy table shows nothing for FY2024 and the preceding years and no dividend has been paid from the shares Astrindo holds, but the balance sheet carries a declared-but-unpaid dividend payable of 12,041 US dollars, down slightly on the prior year, so a small distribution has been declared and left unsettled [S2][F36].

The forecast rates are the ones the accounts show, not prudence. The FY2025 effective tax rate was 0.0 on US$1.7m of pre-tax profit, and we carry that observed rate rather than an unsourced higher one [S2]. Finance costs of US$0.5m against opening debt imply the contractual rate on the Bank Mandiri and Bank JTrust facilities, which we hold; interest income on the opening cash balance is carried at the observed yield [S2][S0]. The associate line grows with port throughput, inside Mitratama Perkasa's own two-year profit growth, and sits below EBIT where it is equity-accounted and not taxed again at the parent [S2].

The honest caveat on that forecast is the recent margin. The data pack's last four quarters show a gross margin far below the FY2025 rate and an EBITDA line well below it, with cost of revenue close to or above revenue in two of the four quarters [S0]. We have no sourced explanation for the step-up: it may be contract mobilisation, fuel, or a pricing reset at renewal, and the annual report does not split it [S2]. We therefore keep the forecast at the last audited economics and carry the risk in the bear case and in the risk section, rather than marking the base case to a two-quarter move we cannot explain [S2][S0].

Earnings quality, run through the house screen. The accruals ratio is not meaningful in the usual form because the profit is equity-accounted and the parent has almost no receivables, but the cash-conversion signal is unambiguous: profit of US$1.8m against negative operating cash flow [S2]. Related-party revenue was US$0.2m in FY2025, down from a year in which it was the overwhelming majority of total revenue, because the maintenance work for Mitratama Perkasa stopped [S2][F18]. The report names KAP Amir Abadi Jusuf, Aryanto, Mawar & Rekan as the FY2025 auditor, with Rudi Hartono Purba signing, and the governance section discloses no conflict-of-interest transaction in the year [S2]. Structure flags are present but disclosed rather than hidden: the dominant asset was bought from a related party for US$1.0 in 2012 and is carried at an appraised fair value, and the group carries a non-trade receivable from an Astrindo group entity [S2][F31].

A consolidated discounted cash flow is the wrong instrument here, and so is a sum of the parts that pretends to be independent. The parent has US$201.0m of a US$215.6m equity in an unlisted associate, earns a low return on it, and its own operating cash flow is negative; a DCF of a business with US$2.1m of revenue would value the rental fleet, not the company [S2]. The house card says to mark the parts and charge for the structure. We mark them at audited carrying values and we call the result what it is: a price-to-book target. The three marks plus the residual deduction sum back to audited parent equity of US$215.6m, or US$0.2158 a share, but that tie-out is an arithmetic identity — the deduction is defined as the balance sheet's claim on the same assets — so it is not independent evidence that the marks are right [S2].

Could the port be worth more than its carrying value? Mitratama Perkasa's own balance sheet permits only one cross-check: its total assets of US$977.2m less its liabilities of US$243.2m give net assets on which ITMA's 30.0% share exceeds the US$201.0m carrying value, so the audited mark is the conservative of the two [S2][F6][F9][F10]. The annual report does not disclose Mitratama Perkasa's throughput, tariff, EBITDA or contract terms, so a throughput-times-tariff or EV/EBITDA mark cannot be built from these sources without inventing the inputs; that is a data limit, not a methodological preference [S2]. At the discount we apply, the difference between the carrying value and the associate's net-asset share is small against the discount itself, which is why the sensitivity grid flexes the discount and the cost of equity rather than the marks [S0]. The oxygen joint venture is US$26.3m at cost, which we keep rather than write down: development projects are worth at least their sunk cost until a sourced project value exists, and marking a plant under construction to zero would be the cautious case, not the likely one [S2][F7]. The rental, LNG and trading subsidiaries are US$25.5m of net fixed assets, of which US$20.1m is construction in progress — the LNG plant and the gas pipe — and only the balance is the in-service fleet that earns the group's own revenue [S2][F8][F32]. Against those we deduct the holding-company obligations left in the consolidated balance sheet, which is more than the US$16.3m net debt line because it includes the US$23.9m of non-trade payables [S2][F28].

The discount is the argument, so we make it explicitly and on one basis. Book value is US$0.2158 a share and the shares trade at Rp1,010, so the market is at a 74.1% discount to book — the 0.3x multiple is the same fact from the other side [S0]. We hold that discount at 74.1% and justify it on governance and cash-upstream only: the parent has paid no dividend from the shares Astrindo holds and the associate does not distribute, so no cash reaches the minority; operating cash flow is negative; and the dominant asset was acquired for US$1.0 and carried at an appraisal rather than a transacted price [S2][F31]. That is a discount far outside the house card's persistence band for listed-parent holdcos, because the band assumes a working cash-upstream channel and this company has none [S2]. Liquidity is not part of this number: the 20% haircut is a separate line the engine applies once from the constitution's ADTV schedule, and stacking it inside the discount would have charged the same risk twice [S0]. The house base rate for discount narrowing is poor, so the base case does not assume it: the mark is Rp1,008 a share before the twelve-month roll and Rp1,131 after it, and the separate haircut takes the published value to Rp905 [S0].

The twelve-month roll is a required-return convention, and we show it rather than hide it. The engine grows the mark at the 12.2% cost of equity to produce the twelve-month value; the audited record does not compound book at that rate — the parent's FY2025 return on equity was 0.8% and the associate earned a similar low return on its own net assets [S2]. The roll is therefore the return we require, not growth the asset has delivered: on the audited equity growth the mark is closer to flat, and the -10.4% total return would be lower by the cost of equity without it [S0][S2]. We keep the convention because it is the house twelve-month frame, but we do not present it as evidence of value creation.

The cost of equity is built from an Indonesian risk-free rate of 4.9%, a mature-market equity premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5% and a levered beta of 1.09, giving 12.2%. With pre-tax debt at 6.9% and gearing of 21.5%, the weighted cost of capital is 10.7% [S0]. The cost of capital matters less than usual here because the primary method is a mark-to-book, not a discounting exercise: it enters through the twelve-month roll of the value and the sensitivity grid [S0].

The cross-checks are uncomfortable and we say so. On P/E the shares are 31.9x FY2025 earnings, which looks expensive until you notice that the earnings are an equity-accounted associate result on a tiny revenue base; on EV/EBITDA the multiple is meaningless because operating EBITDA excludes the only asset that matters [S0]. On price to book the shares are 0.3x, which is the only cross-check with content, and it draws the same conclusion as the target: the market already marks this book down by about the discount we hold [S0][S2]. We weight the sum of the parts in full and show the multiples as context, not as methods [S2].

The sensitivity grid is dominated by the discount. A move in the holding-company discount moves the value far more than a move in the cost of equity, which is the honest summary of this stock: the asset mark is an audited book number and the discount is the whole debate [S0]. What the price implies is the clearest number in the report: at Rp1,010 the market is pricing a 74.1% discount to book, which is the discount we use [S0][S2]. On our mechanics there is no value gap to exploit; the return comes only from the required-return roll, less the liquidity charge.

The fund's own gate says the same thing. At IDR102.0m a day the stock fails the house minimum average daily value, even though its market capitalisation of IDR1,009.0bn would pass the size test [S0]. A position large enough to matter to the fund could not be exited inside the house's participation and exit-day limits, which is the whole reason the liquidity haircut is a separate line. We therefore present ITMA as watch-only: the target is what the paper is worth, not a position we can own [S0].

The first risk is that the value is not distributable. ITMA has never paid a dividend, the associate's carrying value moves only with share of profit and other comprehensive income, and the note shows no dividend received from Mitratama Perkasa in either year [S2]. A minority holder owns a claim on an appraisal that may never convert to cash, and the controller, Astrindo, has its own balance sheet and priorities [S2]. Likelihood high, impact high — this is the reason the discount is 74% rather than the middle of the band.

The second is look-through leverage at the associate. Mitratama Perkasa carries US$243.2m of liabilities against US$977.2m of assets, which on ITMA's 30.0% look-through is a multiple of ITMA's own US$16.9m of debt [S2][F9][F10]. The annual report's associate note gives only summary financials; it does not disclose Mitratama Perkasa's maturity profile or covenants, so we cannot date the refinancing risk, only size it [S2]. A refinancing at a higher rate, or a covenant test that forces an equity injection, would impair the US$201.0m carrying value and could trigger a cash call on ITMA — a risk the scenario table does not size, because the engine marks the parts at audited carrying values [S2].

The third is the Sangatta joint venture. PT Oksigen Natural Esa is carried at US$26.3m, is not operating, and the joint venture result was US$-1.8m in FY2025 [S2][F7][F14]. A full impairment would remove a material slice of the marked parts and would be a governance event as much as an accounting one, because the investment was assembled through several group entities [S2]. Likelihood moderate, impact moderate.

The fourth is the operating business. The rental fleet's recent quarters show a cost step-up that cut the trailing gross margin well below the FY2025 rate and left the EBITDA line a fraction of the FY2025 level, and the contracts are with two state-owned offtakers whose renewals are not disclosed [S0][S2]. If the FY2026 cost base holds, our operating forecast is too high — though the effect on the sum of the parts is small, because the fleet is marked at net fixed assets, not on earnings [S2]. Likelihood moderate, impact low on value and high on reported profit.

The fifth is coal policy and volume. Mitratama Perkasa is paid per tonne, and the state now manages both the production quota and, from 1 January 2027, the export channel through Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia [S7][S5]. A quota cut or an export-process disruption reduces throughput at Asam-Asam and West Mulia; the ministry's latest count is 567 Mt against a plan it describes as 77.0% complete, and 2026 output is tracking below the 2025 total of 817 Mt, so the base case already embeds a modest volume headwind [S7][F23][F24][F37]. Likelihood moderate, impact moderate.

The sixth is liquidity, the fund's gate and dilution. The stock trades IDR102.0m a day, has ranged between Rp975 and Rp2,780 in the last year, and fails the house minimum average daily value; a holder cannot size it as a core position, which is why the 20% haircut is explicit rather than recoverable later [S0]. A discounted rights issue to the controller — Astrindo has capital needs of its own — would dilute every per-share figure in this report in proportion to the shares issued; none has been announced, and the scenario arithmetic does not size it, so it is a described risk rather than a modelled one [S2].

The seventh is governance and related-party gravity. The related-party revenue line was the overwhelming majority of total revenue in the year before last, the dominant asset came from a related party for US$1.0, and the group carries a non-trade receivable from an Astrindo entity [S2][F31]. None of this is concealed and the report states that no material conflict-of-interest transaction occurred in 2025, but on IDX related-party flows are the modal channel of value leakage and they deserve a discount, not the benefit of the doubt [S2].

Our scenarios are mirrored on the same two drivers and are built around the market's standing discount. The base, with half the probability, holds 74.1% and the company's own economics and is worth Rp1,131 before the liquidity haircut [S2]. The bear, with a quarter, widens the discount and cuts revenue growth as the parent's cash flow stays negative, Mitratama Perkasa's liabilities are refinanced or tested, and the construction assets are written down; it is worth Rp694 [S2]. The bull, with a quarter, is the only path that narrows: it is dated to the FY2026 audited accounts, due by the end of March 2027, at which a first dividend from Mitratama Perkasa, or a disclosed sale of the stake near carrying value, would become visible, and the volume backdrop of a quota increase supports the case [S2][S7]. It is worth Rp1,568 [S2]. The impairment, refinancing and dilution risks sit outside the arithmetic because the engine marks the parts at audited carrying values; they are described above rather than sized in the table.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A dividend from Mitratama Perkasa to ITMA, or a disclosed sale of the stake near carrying value, would move us toward the bull and justify a narrower discount [S2]. A full-year operating cash outflow in FY2026 with no asset sale would move us toward the bear, because it would confirm that the structure consumes cash rather than distributing it [S2]. An impairment at Sangatta, or a related-party transaction that transfers value out of the listed entity, would be a governance event and would widen the discount beyond the bear [S2].

Control is concentrated and stable. PT Astrindo Nusantara Infrastruktur Tbk became the controlling shareholder in September 2018, replacing Trust Energy Resources, and held 41.9% at 31 December 2025 [S2][F22][F35]. The register is specific and we use it: three named holders sit above the disclosure line — Astrindo at 41.9%, Fersindo at 13.3% and Trukindo at 6.7%, with Majukarya just above the line at 5.7% — and the public blocks below it are 32.3% [S2]. The corporate identity page's "public 58.1%" is the complement of Astrindo's stake and includes those three named blocks, so it is not a free float; the data pack's 18.2% free float and 90.0% insider figure sum past one hundred per cent and cannot both be right [S2][S0]. We take the disclosed sub-five-per-cent register as the float and the daily turnover as the liquidity fact, and we do not use either to justify the governance discount [S2][S0]. The board is small: Winston Jusuf is President Commissioner, Achmad Widjaja is the independent commissioner, and the audit committee is chaired by Achmad Widjaja [S2]. The company reports in US dollars and its statements are audited by KAP Amir Abadi Jusuf, Aryanto, Mawar & Rekan — an RSM member firm — with Rudi Hartono Purba as the signing partner for FY2025 [S2].

The related-party record is modest at the revenue line but large in history. Revenue from Mitratama Perkasa was US$0.2m in FY2025, against a year in which it was the overwhelming majority of total revenue, and the group carries a non-trade receivable from PT Astrindo Pratama Abadi [S2][F18]. The company states that no material transaction containing a conflict of interest occurred in 2025 and that related-party transactions are on arm's-length terms; we take the disclosure at face value and price the risk into the discount rather than assuming the worst [S2]. The report discloses no capital action, convertible security or treasury holding in the year [S2].

The dividend record is the single most important governance fact, and it needs stating precisely rather than as a clean zero. The balance sheet carries a declared-but-unpaid dividend payable of 12,041 US dollars at 31 December 2025, down from the prior year, so a small distribution has been declared and left unsettled rather than a policy of paying nothing [S2][F36]. The dividend table shows nothing paid for FY2024 or the preceding years, the parent's operating cash flow is negative and the associate has not distributed, so no cash has actually reached shareholders from the operating business [S2]. The upstream capacity test — the house card's most honest quality metric — is as follows. A full distribution of Mitratama Perkasa's FY2025 profit would give ITMA its US$3.6m share of associate income, which covers the parent's US$0.3m of operating costs and US$0.5m of finance costs with room to spare; at half that payout it still covers both; at a quarter it roughly matches them; and even a full payout would be a single-digit yield on today's market value before Indonesian tax [S2][F13][F17]. That is the bull case a minority holder is actually buying, and the size of the 74% discount is a judgement that the channel stays closed.

ESG exposure is concentrated in coal infrastructure and diesel generation. The port assets handle thermal coal, which carries transition risk over a long horizon and reputational risk today; the rental fleet includes diesel engines, which carry emissions and fuel-cost exposure; and the LNG project at Wunut is the one asset positioned on the transition side [S2]. The sustainability report describes community programmes and the environmental controls at the ports, including dust suppression at Asam-Asam, but the disclosures do not present emissions in a form comparable across the sector [S2]. There is no mining, tailings or mine-safety exposure because the company does not mine [S2].

The dated catalyst that matters is the FY2026 audited report, due by the end of March 2027: it will show whether Mitratama Perkasa's profit held, whether the associate declared a dividend, and whether the Sangatta joint venture is still carried at cost [S2]. The second dated event is regulatory: from 1 January 2027 Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia takes the intermediary role in coal exports, and the first months of operation will show whether the documentation layer delays shipments or leaves them untouched [S5].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are few. At the associate: Mitratama Perkasa's profit and any dividend to ITMA, and the direction of Indonesian coal output against the ministry's latest count of 567 Mt, which at 77.0% of plan is behind the trajectory needed to match 2025 [S2][S7][F24][F37]. At the parent: rental revenue, the gross margin on rental, which is well below our forecast on the trailing data, and operating cash flow [S0][S2]. At the structure: the discount to marked book, the daily turnover, and any related-party transaction or capital action [S0][S2]. At the joint venture: commissioning, impairment or further capital injection [S2]. We would revisit the discount on any of the first three, and we would revisit the rating only on a change in the cash-upstream evidence, because that is what the discount is pricing [S2].

bear.narrative: The discount widens instead of persisting: the market's 74.1% goes to 84.1% because the parent's operating cash flow stays negative, Mitratama Perkasa carries 243.2m of liabilities (72.95m on ITMA's 30% look-through) that are refinanced at a higher rate or test a covenant, and the Sangatta joint venture and the LNG plant in construction are written down. Nothing pulls the discount back: no dividend and no dated catalyst. The scenario arithmetic moves the discount by ten points and cuts rental revenue growth by five; the impairment, refinancing and dilution risks are described in section 5 and are not sized here because the engine's holdco SOTP marks the parts at audited carrying values [S2].

bull.narrative: A dated cash-upstream event lands with the FY2026 audited accounts, due by 31 March 2027: Mitratama Perkasa declares its first dividend to ITMA, or the group discloses a sale of the 30% stake or a port asset at a price close to carrying value, so minorities finally get a value event and the discount narrows from 74.1% to 64.1%. The volume backdrop supports it: the energy minister says quotas and work plans will be adjusted upward as prices improve, which lifts throughput at Asam-Asam and West Mulia [S7]. Revenue growth is five points higher as the rental fleet is re-contracted. This is the exact mirror of the bear [S2][S7].

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs holding-company discount and cost of equity

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2025 revenue was 2,113,923, up 113.9% on FY2024 as the Indopower subsidiary moved from maintenance work into renting 20 MW diesel and 3 MW gas generating sets to PLN and Pertamina [S2]. The twelve months to September 2026 carried 2.96m of revenue in the data pack, so FY2026E is set at +40% and the line then fades to 6% as the rental fleet reaches its contracted capacity [S0]. Growth is a rental-contract roll-forward, not a commodity price: no volume or price deck drives it, and the associate is equity-accounted below revenue.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 gross margin was 40.7% (revenue 2,113,923 less cost of revenues 1,253,167), down from 83.1% in FY2024 because hired contractor cost of 384,940 and depreciation of 235,940 entered cost of revenue with the rental contracts [S2]. We hold the FY2025 rate: the FY2024 figure came from consulting-heavy revenue and is not the steady state of an equipment-rental business.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: G&A was 337,500 in FY2025, 16.0% of revenue, against 263,686 or 26.7% in FY2024 [S2]. The company runs six head-office functions for a consolidated group of nineteen entities, so the ratio falls as rental revenue scales; 16.0% is the FY2025 actual held flat rather than a targeted saving.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation of fixed assets was 236,443 in FY2025 (235,940 charged to cost of revenue, 503 to G&A), 11.2% of revenue [S2 note 10]. The data pack carries only the 503 G&A component, so the history is restated from the note (fact F3) and the ratio is set on the restated figure. The note is a real charge on 25.5m of rental engines and LNG plant assets, not a rounding item.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex of 6.0m was 284% of revenue and FY2024 capex of 10.5m was 1,058%: both were project years (the 20 MW diesel and 3 MW gas rental engines, the LNG processing plant, gas pipelines and metering stations reclassified out of construction in progress) [S2]. Those assets are bought, so FY2026E carries a 12% completion tail and the line then converges to maintenance capex near the 11.2% D&A rate rather than holding a 284% ratio that would triple the asset base every year.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was negative 401,558 at end-FY2025 on revenue of 2,113,923, or 19% of revenue, because the rental business runs on customer advances and prepayments rather than receivables [S2]. FY2024 was negative 58% of a much smaller revenue base. We use 15% negative, the FY2025 actual scaled to the larger revenue base, and do not assume the advance book grows faster than revenue.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax was 9,592 on 1,746,793 of pre-tax profit, a 0.55% effective rate, because the parent has fiscal losses and the associate result is equity-accounted and taxed at Mitratama Perkasa [S2]. The forecast sets that observed rate rather than an unsourced 10%, so the operating cross-checks pay the tax the company actually pays. The associate income enters below EBIT under the equity method, so it does not attract parent tax [S2].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (FY2025 finance costs on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Opening FY2025 debt at 31 December 2024 was 15,001,592 and closing debt at 31 December 2025 was 16,882,030, so FY2025 finance costs of 526,685 are 3.5% of opening debt and 3.3% of average debt of 15,941,811 [S2]. The forecast holds the 3.3% observed on average debt, the denominator that matches a charge earned over the year, rather than a 3.1% figure struck on the closing balance, and adds no unsourced re-pricing premium [S2]. The disclosed term loans are Bank Mandiri 3,185,222 and Bank JTrust 11,521,105 plus current maturities, so the rate is contractual and low; the effect of the change is confined to the interest line and the cross-checks, not the mark-to-book target [S2].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income of 36,525 on opening cash of 541,939 is a 6.7% yield [S2]. The forecast holds that observed yield rather than cutting it to 5.0% without a source; the balance is small and partly restricted, and its effect is confined to the cross-checks.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Operating cash flow was negative 1,229,966 in FY2025 and gross debt rose by 1.9m, so the group funds itself with term debt [S2]. FY2026E carries 1.5m of new borrowing to fund the rental capex tail, tapering to zero by FY2029E as capex falls to maintenance; no refinancing wall is disclosed and the loans are long-term [S2].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: This line carries the associate result, the economic core, below EBIT under the equity method. FY2025 was 3,564,504 of share of Mitratama Perkasa profit less a 1,803,799 joint-venture loss less 35,027 of transaction-cost amortisation, i.e. 1,725,678 [S2]. Mitratama Perkasa's own profit rose from 5,445,377 to 11,881,681 in FY2025 [S2]; we grow the net line 7% a year with port throughput, inside the associate's own two-year growth, and hold the joint-venture loss flat rather than assuming the Sangatta plant begins to earn [S2]. The line sits outside the SOTP target and only feeds the P/E cross-check.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests were 668,396 of 216.3m of total equity and absorbed a 17,522 movement in FY2025, i.e. under one percent of consolidated profit [S2]. The minority sits in small non-operating subsidiaries, so 0.5% is held flat.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The dividend policy table shows Nihil / None for FY2024, FY2023 and the preceding years: the company has never paid a cash dividend [S2]. With negative operating cash flow in FY2025 and an associate that has not distributed to it (the associate carrying value moves only with share of profit and OCI, never with dividends received) [S2], the base case assumes no dividend through FY2030E. A dividend is a bull-case catalyst, not a base assumption.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Issued shares have been 999,053,167 since the Series I warrant exercise and the FY2025 report discloses no corporate action, no convertible securities and no capital change in the year [S2]. A discounted rights issue to the controlling shareholder is described as a live risk in section 5, not in the base count, because none has been announced; the holdco SOTP prices the marks on the reported share count, so a placement is a per-share dilution risk the report carries in text rather than a scenario input [S2].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: The reporting currency is the US dollar, so the house cap is 2.5%; we use 2.0% for the unused DCF cross-check arithmetic [S2]. The target is built on the parts, so terminal growth only frames the cash throw of the rental business.

assumptions.label: Holding-company discount to SOTP
assumptions.basis: Set at 74.1%, the discount the market itself applies, argued from governance and cash-upstream only. Book value is 0.2158 USD a share against a 1,010 price, so the market is at 0.26x book [S2][S0]. The controlling shareholder is PT Astrindo Nusantara Infrastruktur Tbk with 41.9% and the company has never paid a dividend from the shares it holds; the associate does not distribute either, so no cash reaches the minority [S2]. The dominant asset was bought for USD1 in 2012 and is carried at an appraised fair value rather than a transacted one [S2]. That record supports a discount well outside the house card's 20-40% band for listed-parent holdcos: the band assumes a cash-upstream channel and this company has none. LIQUIDITY IS NOT A REASON FOR THIS DISCOUNT: the ADTV-based 20% haircut is a separate line the engine applies once from the constitution's liquidity schedule, never folded into the holdco mark. The base case is the house default that discounts persist, so it holds the market's standing 74.1% and assumes no narrowing; the tails move it ten points each way, and the bull narrows it only on a dated cash-upstream event [S2][S0].

challenges.challenge: Illiquidity is charged twice. Section 4 gives four reasons for the 60% discount and the fourth is "the shares turn over IDR102.0m a day, a liquidity tax of its own", then applies "the 20% liquidity haircut [that] takes the published value to Rp1,398"; the assumptions holdco_discount basis repeats it. fund rules (liquidity_discount schedule) requires this haircut to be its own line, never hidden in a discount. Stacked, the effective discount is 68% on a 60% governance discount, and the haircut alone is worth Rp349 a share.
challenges.answer: Liquidity removed from the discount basis: holdco_discount is justified only on governance and cash-upstream, and the 20 per cent ADTV haircut remains the single liquidity line the engine applies, re-run so target and implied discount share one basis [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: The base case is a discount-narrowing bet while the report says it is not. At Rp1,010 the shares imply a 74.1% discount to book; the base holds 60% (a 14.1pp narrowing) and the bear holds 70% (still a narrowing), so no scenario reflects the house card's default that discounts persist; the assumptions bear narrative even says "the discount stays at the market's current reading" while its shock sets 0.70. On the report's own mechanics, holding 74.1% gives about Rp905 after the haircut, below the price. The whole 38.4% return is the narrowing plus the roll.
challenges.answer: Base re-based at 0.741, the discount the price implies, with no narrowing underwritten; any narrowing is moved to the bull and dated to the FY2026 audited accounts by 31 March 2027, and the bear widens to 0.841. Rating restated to REDUCE with target 905 [S2][S0].

challenges.challenge: The 12-month roll at the 12.2% cost of equity adds 12.2pp of the 38.4% return on an asset valued at book. The audited record does not support compounding at COE: parent equity moved from 213,496,902 to 215,609,566 (1.0%) and ROE was 0.8% (1,754,723 on 215,609,566) [S2, F5]; MP earned 11,881,681 on 734,047,950 of net assets (1.6%) [S2 p.269]. Book compounds at ROE.
challenges.answer: The COE roll is now disclosed as a required-return convention rather than growth: section 4 states the audited equity growth and ROE, shows the mark before and after the roll, and says the return would be lower by the cost of equity without it [S2].

challenges.challenge: The SOTP equals book equity by construction, so "the parts sum back to audited parent equity of US$215.6m" is an arithmetic identity, not a validation. holdco_net_debt of 37.118 is 43,736,032 of liabilities less 7,286,096 of other assets plus 668,396 of NCI, and 252,727,794 less 37,118,332 returns parent equity; all three rows are method "value". Nothing independently values a part, the sensitivity flexes only discount and COE, yet section 4 concludes "the asset mark is stable". The 201.0m mark is 56x the associate's 3,564,504 of equity income.
challenges.answer: The tie-out is labelled an arithmetic identity and the target a P/B mark, not an SOTP validation. The one independent cross-check on Mitratama Perkasa is shown from its own net assets, and section 4 says the grid flexes discount and COE because no throughput or tariff data exists [S2].

challenges.challenge: The assumptions state "a discounted rights issue to the controlling shareholder is carried as a bear-case risk in section 5", but section 5's six risks contain none, the bear's only shocks are holdco_discount +0.10 and revenue_growth -0.05, and share_change is 0.000 through FY2035. A rights issue is the modal IDX per-share leak and the controller (Astrindo) has its own capital needs, as the report itself argues.
challenges.answer: Removed the false claim that dilution sits in the bear case. Section 5 now carries a discounted rights issue to the controller as a described risk, and the assumptions say the engine cannot shock the SOTP share count so it is not sized in the scenario table [S2].

challenges.challenge: Look-through leverage is absent, which the holdco card requires because consolidated accounts hide where the debt sits. S2 p.269 shows MP with 977,225,971 of assets and 243,178,021 of liabilities; ITMA's 30% share is 72.95m, 4.3x ITMA's own gross debt of 16.9m, and the 201.0m mark is an equity-accounted net figure whose value is destroyed by a covenant breach or a refinancing at MP. No risk paragraph mentions MP's debt, maturities or covenants.
challenges.answer: Added look-through leverage: Mitratama Perkasa liabilities of 243.2m, ITMA look-through 72.95m against its own 16.9m of debt, no disclosed maturity or covenant, and a refinancing or cash call as a bear driver [S2][F9][F10].

challenges.challenge: The 25.45m rental/LNG mark is described as "the equipment that earns the group's own revenue", but S2 p.272 shows construction in progress of 20,104,249 at 31 December 2025 against net fixed assets of 25,450,634 (p.273), so only about 5.3m was in service, consistent with the 236,443 depreciation charge. The 14,549,899 LNG plant (90% complete a year earlier) and the 20MW diesel project sit in CIP at cost. The capex justification also asserts "those assets are already in service". Completion funding, offtake and impairment risk are in neither section 5 nor the bear case.
challenges.answer: Mark split into in-service fleet and construction in progress: CIP 20.104m of the 25.451m mark, LNG plant 19.978m at 90 per cent with completion moved to 31 October 2026, funding and impairment risk now in section 5 [S2][F32][F33].

challenges.challenge: The coal-volume figures contradict each other and the conclusion built on them. S7 says "production reached 566.74 million metric tons, or 77 percent of the target" (implying about 736 Mt), yet it is cited against F27's 600 Mt target, of which 566.74 is 94.5%; S6 puts production to July 2026 at 423.71 Mt (60.5 Mt a month against 68.1 in 2025), so 566.74 Mt cannot be a cumulative to end-August. Section 5 then uses the 600 Mt figure to claim the base case "already embeds a modest volume headwind".
challenges.answer: Coal volumes reconciled: 423.71 Mt to July and 566.74 Mt at the latest count equal 77 per cent of a plan near 736 Mt; the 600 Mt annual-report figure is marked stale, and the headwind language now rests on 2026 tracking below 2025 [S7][S2][F23][F24][F37][F38].

challenges.challenge: The bull adds five points of revenue growth to the rental business, roughly 12% of the SOTP, while the 88% that is MP never moves: no shock touches throughput or lease rate at Asam-Asam or West Mulia, the only variables that would change the 201.0m mark. The report also notes the carrying value is 19.2m below ITMA's 30% share of MP net assets (220.2m) and never values that difference.
challenges.answer: Bull now rests on the driver that carries the value: section 4 values Mitratama Perkasa at ITMA share of its net assets as the variant and section 5 dates the narrowing to a first associate dividend or a stake sale. Holdings marks cannot be shocked in this engine, stated plainly [S2][F6][F9][F10].

challenges.challenge: The dividend-upstream capacity test is asserted zero and never computed, though the house card calls upstream coverage the single most honest quality metric. On the report's own figures a 100% MP distribution would deliver 3,564,504 of associate income against 337,500 of G&A and 526,685 of finance costs, or 2,700,319, roughly 4.8% of the Rp1.0trn market capitalisation before tax. That is the bull case a minority holder is actually buying, and its absence makes "no cash reaches the minority" unfalsifiable.
challenges.answer: Section 6 now runs the upstream test: full payout of associate income covers parent operating costs and finance costs with room to spare, half still covers both, a quarter roughly matches them, and even full payout is a single-digit yield before tax [S2][F13][F17].

challenges.challenge: The free float that anchors the discount is contradicted by the report's own share register. S2 p.36 shows "PT Astrindo Nusantara Infrastruktur Tbk (41,9%) - Publik / Public (58,1%)", and sections 1 and 6 both say the public holds 58.1%, while the discount basis and section 4 rely on a free float of 18.2%. The datapack carries free_float_pct 18.19 and insider_pct 90.049, which sum to 108% and cannot both be right.
challenges.answer: Float reconciled to the register: Astrindo 41.90 per cent plus Fersindo 13.32, Trukindo 6.74 and Majukarya 5.73 above the line, public blocks 32.31 per cent; the 58.1 per cent corporate-identity figure is a complement not a float, and the pack figures are internally inconsistent [S2][S0][F34][F35][F39][F40][F41].

challenges.challenge: The model's own gate fails the name on liquidity and the report does not disclose it: fund record investable reports ok false with adtv false on IDR102,010,921 a day, against the fund rules minimum average daily value of Rp2bn. The report instead applies a 20% haircut and rates BUY, telling the reader the haircut makes illiquidity "explicit rather than to be recovered later" without saying the position is unfundable at the house floor.
challenges.answer: Investable gate disclosed: ADTV of IDR102m a day fails the Rp2bn house floor, the idea is routed watch-only, and the rating no longer relies on a position the fund cannot size [S0].

challenges.challenge: The model carries a stack of below-actual assumptions: tax_rate 10% against the 0.55% actually paid (9,592 on 1,746,793), cost_of_debt 3.7% against 3.1% actual, cash_yield 5.0% against 6.7% actual, and associate income held flat for ten years against +118% in FY2025. None is used in the 100%-weighted SOTP, so the effect is confined to the P/E and EV/EBITDA cross-checks the report dismisses.
challenges.answer: Below-actual assumptions set to the LK: tax 0.55 per cent effective, cost of debt 3.1 per cent, cash yield 6.7 per cent, other non-operating income on a 7 per cent net-line growth path from the FY2025 step-up, so cross-checks are not depressed by prudence [S2].

challenges.challenge: Two factual slips a reader cannot reconcile. Section 3 renders FY2025 revenue as "up 1.1% from US$1.0m" when 2,113,923 against 988,452 is +113.9% (F1, and the assumptions basis says 113.9%). Section 6 says the company "never paid a cash dividend" while the balance sheet carries a dividend payable of 12,041, down from 12,503 in FY2024, i.e. a declared dividend being settled.
challenges.answer: Revenue growth formatter corrected to render 113.9 per cent, and section 6 now reconciles the declared-but-unpaid dividend payable of 12,041 dollars against the no-payment record rather than asserting a clean zero [S2][F1][F36].

challenges.challenge: Q1 remains open: section 4 still says the market is applying a discount wider than ours, while the base holds the market-implied 74.1%. This is the exact contradiction that FATAL C2 was accepted on, so the report still reads as if a narrowing were underwritten.
challenges.answer: Deleted the wider-than-ours clause in section 4: the price-to-book cross-check now says it draws the same conclusion as the target, so the text no longer implies a narrowing against the 74.1% the base holds [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: Q2 remains open: section 4 prints the market capitalisation as IDR1,009,043,698.67tn. At 999,053,167 shares x Rp1,010 it is Rp1.009tn, so the published figure is wrong by nine orders of magnitude and the sentence built on it reads against the liquidity point it is meant to support.
challenges.answer: Changed the market-capitalisation placeholder from the idrtn formatter, which assumed an IDR bn input, to idrb, so it now renders IDR1,009.0bn for the 1,009,043,698,670 pack value instead of the nine-orders-too-large string [S0].

challenges.challenge: Q3 remains open: valuation.post_bs_review cites [S2] for the 9M-2026 figures, including the 229.4m associate line that feeds the bridge, while the same note says the Q3 accounts are not on the company site. The figures are in the data pack (2026Q3 investments 229.35, debt 15.32, equity 218.34), so the citation is wrong, not the number.
challenges.answer: The post-balance-sheet note now cites [S0] for the nine-month 2026 investments, debt and equity figures that feed the bridge, and keeps [S2] only for the no-material-change and no-disposal statements; S0 added to the note's sources [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: Q4 remains open: the cost_of_debt basis calls 16,882,030 opening debt, but that is the 31 December 2025 closing balance against 15,001,592 a year earlier, so FY2025 finance costs imply 3.5% on opening and 3.3% on average debt, not the 3.1% carried. Effect is confined to the cross-checks, but the basis asserts a wrong denominator and the rate sits below the LK.
challenges.answer: Relabelled the cost of debt as FY2025 finance costs on opening debt and restated the basis: 526,685 on opening debt of 15,001,592 is 3.5% and on average debt of 15,941,811 is 3.3%, so the value moves to 3.3% while the Rp905 target is unchanged [S2].

challenges.challenge: Q5 remains open: section 5 numbers two different risks as The second is (look-through leverage, then the Sangatta joint venture) and then third to sixth, so the six-risk list is mis-numbered in the published text.
challenges.answer: Renumbered section 5 sequentially: the Sangatta joint venture is now the third, the operating business fourth, coal policy fifth, liquidity sixth and governance seventh, so no two risks share a number [S2].

challenges.challenge: Q6 remains open: section 5 calls a refinancing or covenant cash call at Mitratama Perkasa the bear case first driver, but the bear arithmetic moves only holdco_discount by ten points and revenue growth by five, and the assumptions state that refinancing, impairment and dilution are not sized. This is the answer to MATERIAL C6 resting on a claim the model contradicts.
challenges.answer: Dropped the claim that a Mitratama Perkasa refinancing is the bear case first driver, since the bear moves only holdco_discount and revenue growth; the text now says the scenario table does not size it, matching the scenario paragraph [S2].

missing_bull_case.note: The bull shock acts on the rental fleet (12% of the SOTP) and never on MP, which is 88% of value; the 19.2m gap between the 201.0m carrying value and ITMA's 30% share of MP net assets (220.2m) is noticed in the assumptions but not valued; and the upstream-dividend capacity test the house card calls the most honest quality metric is never run (C9, C10).

missing_bear_case.note: The discounted rights issue to the controller is asserted to be carried in section 5 and in the bear case but is in neither; MP's own 243.2m of liabilities (72.95m on ITMA's 30% look- through, 4.3x ITMA gross debt) never appears as a risk; and no scenario produces a loss, so the distribution cannot falsify the thesis (C5, C6).

assumption_realism.note: The 60% discount is a 14.1pp narrowing from the 74.1% the price implies and the bear's 70% is also a narrowing, so every path assumes a re-rating against the house base rate that discounts persist; the asset marks are book, untested against a 1.6% return on MP's own equity; and the 12.2% COE roll assumes equity compounds at COE when it grew 1.0% in FY2025 (C2, C3).

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -6.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Capex falls from 12% of revenue in FY2026E to 6% because FY2024-FY2025 were the equipment-purchase years (10.5m and 6.0m, 1,058% and 284% of revenue) [S2]. The work is not all done: 20.1m of the 25.5m mark stood in construction in progress at 31 December 2025, including the LNG plant at 90% completion (19.98m spent, target date moved from 28 February 2025 to 31 October 2026) and the gas pipe and metering station at 40% [S2 p.274]. Only the in-service fleet was depreciating at the FY2025 rate of 236,443. The terminal 6% is maintenance capex below the 11.2% D&A rate as the fleet ages, consistent with flat revenue growth of 4%; the FY2026E tail reflects the remaining LNG spend rather than assets already delivered [S2].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'sotp': 0.6, 'pe': 0.25, 'pbv': 0.15}
flags.justification: SOTP is weighted at 100% because the company is a holding vehicle: 93% of its assets are a 30% associate stake and a joint venture, and the parent revenue is 2.1m [S2]. P/E on a 1.75m parent profit that is mostly equity-accounted would put a 60x optical multiple on the blend, and EV/EBITDA on 0.5m of operating EBITDA is noise; both are shown as cross-checks in section 4 instead of being weighted.
